Note: I have done a successful basic run through with BioGeoBEARS and read most of the documentation, but my understanding of the inner workings may still be naïve.

Anne

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] How to use the 'manual_dispersal_multipliers' or to define odds for states/ranges to go through
messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] How to use the 'manual_dispersal_multipliers' or to define odds for states/ranges to go through
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- yes, it is possible. The simplest / most natural way to do it is with a distance matrix rather than manual dispersal multipliers.

You define a matrix of relative distances, where

relative distance = (Great Circle Distance) / (minimum nonzero distance*** between all areas)

Then, you set "x" to be a free parameter, and estimate it along with all of the other parameters during the ML search.  The x parameter modified the base dispersal rates/weights like this:

d_actual = d_base * (relative_distance)^x
j_actual = j_base * (relative_distance)^x

If x is fixed to 0, then the distance has no impact on dispersal probability. This is the null model, and this is what you are already assuming in a standard BioGeoBEARS model with no special multipliers on dispersal probabilities.

If x is free, and inferred to be negative (which is usually the case), then dispersal probability drops off with distance. If x=-1, then doubling the distance halves the dispersal probability.  If x=-2, then dispersal probability drops off with the square of distance.

This method gets you away from the old problem of "how do I objectively decide the manual dispersal multipliers, e.g. should South-America to Africa get a multiplier of 0.1 or 0.001 or what??".  By estimating x, you are estimating the effect of distance on dispersal probability.

This model variant is written up in: Van Dam and Matzke (2016), Journal of Biogeography.

Cheers,
Nick

*** If your minimum distance between 2 areas is 0 because the two areas are touching, you need to think of a slightly more complex solution. E.g., perhaps you use the distances between the center points of regions. Or, perhaps you set the areas-touching distance to 1, and also set the closest nonzero distance to 1, but then use a second matrix (the manual dispersal multiplier matrix) to put a penalty of 0.1 on dispersal when areas are not touching, and then turn on the w parameter and estimate w as a free parameter, so that the parameter for non-touching areas is 0.1^w.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: UPDATE: All BioGeoBEARS code updates now in GitHub package
messages.subject_clean: UPDATE: All BioGeoBEARS code updates now in GitHub package
messages.body_plain:
Hi BioGeoBEARS users,

In recent years, I posted patches and updates to the BioGeoBEARS to the PhyloWiki page, and included source() commands in the example script at http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script to source these updates.

This was convenient as I could just keep the code on Dropbox on my various computers, and code changes would auto-update to all of my machines automatically as I traveled extensively.  It also it meant I could post quick fixes without going through CRAN. CRAN updates were challenging for BioGeoBEARS, because BioGeoBEARS relies on packages rexpokit (which wraps FORTRAN code used by BioGeoBEARS to make calculations run faster) and cladoRcpp (which wraps C++ code).

CRAN packages are very useful, because CRAN produces binary install files that install easily on Windows, Macs, and other machines, without the need for downloading compilers and setting compiler options, which can be a real nightmare e.g. when teaching a workshop to students with diverse computers and computational backgrounds. However, updating CRAN packages that contain FORTRAN or C++ can be very challenging, because CRAN keeps changing its standards as compilers and compiler flags change, and many of the warnings/notes that result have very obscure causes. Over the years, this meant that rexpokit and cladoRcpp accumulated more and more warnings/notes etc. on in CRAN's "R CMD check" function, and it became a very big project to dig back into the arcane details needed to fix up the FORTRAN/C++ source code to pass R CMD check.

Anyway: I have finally gotten around to doing it, so there are now new versions of rexpokit and cladoRcpp on CRAN, and CRAN has also now generated binaries for these. So, everyone should update these packages, with these commands:

# 1. Install the new rexpokit, version 0.26.6 from CRAN:
install.packages('rexpokit')

# 2. Install the new cladoRcpp version 0.15 from CRAN:
install.packages('cladoRcpp')

With these packages installed, all of the BioGeoBEARS updates can be installed from GitHub, rather than re-running the source() commands again and again. This version is being called BioGeoBEARS v1.1, and should be referenced as such. Once BioGeoBEARS is installed from GitHub, you do not have to re-install it again until you want to, and you should delete all of the source() commands that we were using previously.

# 3. Install devtools from CRAN:
install.packages('devtools')

# 4. Install the updated BioGeoBEARS from GitHub, install with:
library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo='nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS')

# 5. Finally, run library() on these packages:
library(rexpokit)
library(cladoRcpp)
library(BioGeoBEARS)

The code updates include the code for Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping, trait-dependent dispersal, etc., previously mentioned on PhyloWiki.

I am working on getting the updated BioGeoBEARS onto CRAN -- including updated help files/documentation, and using CRAN's updated system for linking functions etc. -- but this is less of a priority, as BioGeoBEARS itself is "pure R" and so installs easily from GitHub without any messing around from compilers.

EXPECTED WARNINGS: When you install from GitHub, you will get various warnings about e.g. function linking and the lack of man/help files, but you can ignore these for now.

HELP: If you need help for functions, use Google to find the old help/man pages on CRAN, or search the BioGeoBEARS Google Group.

I will update the various PhyloWiki scripts to remove the source() commands when I get a chance. If run, the source() commands will now all pop up a message giving the above information about the updates and where to find them.

Citation information: A permalink for Version 1.1 is available as a DOI:

Matzke, Nicholas J. (2018). BioGeoBEARS: BioGeography with Bayesian (and likelihood) Evolutionary Analysis with R Scripts. version 1.1, published on GitHub on October 10, 2018. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1463216  GitHub: https://github.com/nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS

Please let me know if you have any problems / installation failures (not just warnings).

Cheers!
Nick Matzke

messages.subject_clean: (anonymised) Use BioGeoBEARS in large phylogeny
messages.body_plain:
Advice on an anonymised question:

On Fri, Oct 19, 2018 at 2:41 AM XXXX wrote:
> Dear Nicholas J. Matzke,
>
> I am a researcher focusing on the macro-evolutionary patterns in some animals. I am now trying to use the BioGeoBEARS package to infer the ancestral distribution of lizards. My phylogeny is a time-tree with 4858 taxa, and the current distribution states of each tip are mapped to 20 regions (max region size = 15), so my GeoData is a 4858*20 matrix. When I test the simplest model (DEC), the calculation crashes immediately. I monitor the system usage, but fail to find any exhausted sources (CPU or memory). I guess it is caused by the large phylogeny, but even the "force_sparse = TRUE" dose not help.
>
> So do you have any idea in this situation? Can I cut the tree into many subtrees with smaller size and achieve the calculations in subtrees first and then try to reconstruct the ancestral states using the pruned stem tree using the results of subtrees as "current states"?
>
> Thanks and best wishes,
> XXXXXX

Dear XXX,

Thank you for writing!  I know the cause of this issue.  It is actually not the size of your phylogeny -- it is the size of your state space.  In biogeographical models, we have a very large number of states, even if we have only 20 areas.  This is because we have every combination of presence/absence as a state.

So, if you have 3 areas, A B C, you have 8 states:

_, A, B, C, AB, AC, BC, ABC

8 states = 2^3

If you have 20 areas, you have 1048576 states, and the transition matrix (Q) is 1048576 x 1048576.  The largest transition matrix I've every seen run was only 2500x2500, and that was very slow.

If you set max_range_size to 15, you still have:

numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=15, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 1042380

...1042380 states, which is almost as huge.

Basically, your only hope in BioGeoBEARS is to merge some areas, or lower the max areas to 3 or lower.  Use the numstates_from_numareas function:

> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=4, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 6196
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=3, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 1351
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=2, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 211
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=1, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 21
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=1, include_null_range=FALSE)
[1] 20

However, you probably have observed some species occupying 15 areas, so this means you instead have to merge some of those areas.

This is a common problem, here is some saved advice:

Question: Too many areas / too many states / BioGeoBEARS too slow. Answers: diverse
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#too_many_areas

=============
So, your only choices are:

1. Reduce areas or max number of areas. Focus on what you think are the "most discrete" features in the geography, i.e. geographical features that are clearly conserved on the phylogeny. IMHO there isn't a huge point in doing ancestral state inference except on things that are pretty conserved on the phylogeny anyway.

1a. One option is to just model the centroid point of each species, thus each species occupies 1 area. You could do up to 1000 or 2000 areas this way, but you are sacrificing whatever is useful about modeling species as widespread (e.g., information about the cladogenetic process). Whether this is important depends on how likely you think it is you will successfully get such information anyway…

2. Use BayArea (the C++ program, not the BAYAREALIKE model in BioGeoBEARS). This means you are assuming BayArea's cladogenesis model (ancestral range always copied exact to both descendants, e.g. assuming widespread sympatry). RevBayes can combine BayArea-type Bayesian history sampling with cladogenesis models, but my understanding is that sampling cladogenetic histories effectively is very difficult, at least for larger problems.

3. Get sparse matrix exponentiation working in BioGeoBEARS or your own program (I can probably get sparse matrix stuff working, it would take me about a solid week which I won't have for awhile. And it might not solve your scale of problem anyway).

4. Be a genius and solve the computational problems in some new way.

5. One option is subdividing the problem into subregions and doing each separately.
=============

The one update I would make is that RevBayes now can do what the old BayArea program did -- but I don't think they've got cladogenesis models working for that large-number-of-areas problem, so you are stuck with "ranges are copied exactly at cladogenesis", i.e. no vicariance, no jump dispersal etc. The BayArea assumptions are diagrammed here (compared to other models):

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic

Advice on choosing meaningful areas:

How to decide your geographic areas
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#how_geog_areas

Cheers,
Nick

PS: See the BioGeoBEARS Google Group about recent code updates, I'm pasting it here if you can't access the Google Group:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/VHOVNUNuHOE
===================
Hi BioGeoBEARS users,

In recent years, I posted patches and updates to the BioGeoBEARS to the PhyloWiki page, and included source() commands in the example script at http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script to source these updates.

This was convenient as I could just keep the code on Dropbox on my various computers, and code changes would auto-update to all of my machines automatically as I traveled extensively.  It also it meant I could post quick fixes without going through CRAN. CRAN updates were challenging for BioGeoBEARS, because BioGeoBEARS relies on packages rexpokit (which wraps FORTRAN code used by BioGeoBEARS to make calculations run faster) and cladoRcpp (which wraps C++ code).

CRAN packages are very useful, because CRAN produces binary install files that install easily on Windows, Macs, and other machines, without the need for downloading compilers and setting compiler options, which can be a real nightmare e.g. when teaching a workshop to students with diverse computers and computational backgrounds. However, updating CRAN packages that contain FORTRAN or C++ can be very challenging, because CRAN keeps changing its standards as compilers and compiler flags change, and many of the warnings/notes that result have very obscure causes. Over the years, this meant that rexpokit and cladoRcpp accumulated more and more warnings/notes etc. on in CRAN's "R CMD check" function, and it became a very big project to dig back into the arcane details needed to fix up the FORTRAN/C++ source code to pass R CMD check.

Anyway: I have finally gotten around to doing it, so there are now new versions of rexpokit and cladoRcpp on CRAN, and CRAN has also now generated binaries for these. So, everyone should update these packages, with these commands:

# 1. Install the new rexpokit, version 0.26.6 from CRAN:
install.packages('rexpokit')

# 2. Install the new cladoRcpp version 0.15 from CRAN:
install.packages('cladoRcpp')

With these packages installed, all of the BioGeoBEARS updates can be installed from GitHub, rather than re-running the source() commands again and again. This version is being called BioGeoBEARS v1.1, and should be referenced as such. Once BioGeoBEARS is installed from GitHub, you do not have to re-install it again until you want to, and you should delete all of the source() commands that we were using previously.

# 3. Install devtools from CRAN:
install.packages('devtools')

# 4. Install the updated BioGeoBEARS from GitHub, install with:
library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo='nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS')

# 5. Finally, run library() on these packages:
library(rexpokit)
library(cladoRcpp)
library(BioGeoBEARS)

The code updates include the code for Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping, trait-dependent dispersal, etc., previously mentioned on PhyloWiki.

I am working on getting the updated BioGeoBEARS onto CRAN -- including updated help files/documentation, and using CRAN's updated system for linking functions etc. -- but this is less of a priority, as BioGeoBEARS itself is "pure R" and so installs easily from GitHub without any messing around from compilers.

EXPECTED WARNINGS: When you install from GitHub, you will get various warnings about e.g. function linking and the lack of man/help files, but you can ignore these for now.

HELP: If you need help for functions, use Google to find the old help/man pages on CRAN, or search the BioGeoBEARS Google Group.

I will update the various PhyloWiki scripts to remove the source() commands when I get a chance. If run, the source() commands will now all pop up a message giving the above information about the updates and where to find them.

Citation information: A permalink for Version 1.1 is available as a DOI:

Matzke, Nicholas J. (2018). BioGeoBEARS: BioGeography with Bayesian (and likelihood) Evolutionary Analysis with R Scripts. version 1.1, published on GitHub on October 10, 2018. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1463216  GitHub: https://github.com/nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS

Please let me know if you have any problems / installation failures (not just warnings).

Cheers!
Nick Matzke

Hi!  Thanks for the question.  I'll give you my sense of all this, which hopefully will help:

1. It looks like both optimx and GenSA work fine, without crashing, if these have all been updated to the new versions:
- R itself
- rexpokit (0.15 from CRAN)
- cladoRcpp (0.26.6 from CRAN)
- BioGeoBEARS (version 1.1 from GitHub).

So: you should be able to use either one.

2. You may get a speedup if you "byte-compile" the BioGeoBEARS package when installing from GitHub -- this might be a speedup of a few times.  Byte-compilation is default from CRAN packages, but perhaps not from GitHub, I'm not sure.  I haven't tested the speed, but the installation from GitHub works with byte-compilation on:

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS", INSTALL_opts="--byte-compile")

3. Also: especially for GenSA, it is useful to have the on_NaN_error option set, like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$on_NaN_error = -1e50

...this means that, if a parameter combination is tried that results in a NaN for the likelihood (usually parameters at the very edges of the parameter limits), instead of returning NaN and crashing the search, instead a lnL of -1e50 is returned, and the search continues.

A few days ago I made this the default setting in 1.1.  This is more important in GenSA, since GenSA does a more thorough search and seems to explore the boundaries of the parameter space as part of this.

4. GenSA definitely takes several times longer than optimx to optimize.  It is doing a more thorough search (in my experience), and so it calculates the likelihood more times.  The benefit of this is that there is a lower chance of find a claimed Maximum Likelihood result that is actually just a local optimum, instead of a global optimum.  My experience is that this is important e.g. in trait-dependent dispersal models (where you have e.g. 6 or 7 free parameters), but not really for the standard DEC vs DEC+J problems with 2 or 3 parameters.  Detailed advice on thinking about your optimization results, and ways to check, here:

Issues with Maximum Likelihood (ML) optimization
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#optim

5. The choice of optimx versus GenSA should not effect the length of individual likelihood calculations, ie individual steps in the ML search.  These should stay the same either way.  What makes GenSA slower is that it is doing more likelihood calculations during the search.

6. The slow step in the likelihood calculation is matrix exponentiation. These are done by rexpokit, which wraps the FORTRAN code EXPOKIT.  As far as I know, this should not have gotten slower in the update -- but, CRAN forced me to make some minor changes to the EXPOKIT source code in order to pass CRAN's checks, and it is vaguely possible (but doesn't seem likely to me) that this could have made the code less efficient.  If people keep seeing this, let me know.

7. One thing that would definitely slow down the likelihood calculations, for large problems, is if parallelization was unavailable on a particular setup (e.g. only 1 core available, R.app only runs on 1 core, etc.).  But, BioGeoBEARS should report how many cores are available and how many are being used.

Cheers!
Nick

On Thursday, October 11, 2018 at 3:43:51 AM UTC+13, anneth...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi Nick,
>
>
> I’m interested in seeing if I can use BioGeoBEARS to address the following question: Which is associated with higher levels of cladogenesis, an increase in similar habitat (eg sea level retreat) or an addition of novel habitat? I’m brainstorming ways to do this, and one idea would require explicit expansion of a given area over time. I saw that there is an area_of_areas feature, but from what I could find (the “areas_allowed and dispersal_multipliers” post) that seems to be focused on extinction/range contraction. Could it be used for the opposite (eg maybe by setting the 'd' parameter to free?), or are the models not designed to handle that?
>
>
> Note: I have done a successful basic run through with BioGeoBEARS and read most of the documentation, but my understanding of the inner workings may still be naïve.
>
>
> Thanks,
>
> Anne

Hi -- this is a complex question.

Re: the "area of areas" feature -- this was coded up to be a modifier on the "e" process (the rate of range contraction aka rate of extirpation in an area).  One can easily imagine, for instance, that this rate would be higher in areas that are smaller.  However, the inference of the "e" parameter is so poor in most models, that I never seriously pursued trying to infer modifiers for "e".

Background on inference of "e" :

1. Poor inference of "e" was noted in Ree & Smith 2008 for the DEC model

2. It seems to be similarly poor in most other models -- the basic problems are

2a. transitions like A->null and B->null are allowed in the model, but the "null range" is almost never observed in actual data.  As the null range is never observed, the inference "thinks" that the rate of going from A->null, B->null, etc., must be low, therefore "e" must be low (usually 0).  There are some exceptions, e.g. if you have many species occupying 2, 3, 4 etc. ranges, but this is fairly rare

2b. in a sense, the "e" process is competing with vicariance etc. as ways to "reduce range size", since the cladogenesis processes typically produce average ranges smaller than the parent range, it is hard to get signal for e

3. Inference of "e" probably works better in a model like BAYAREALIKE model (but not BAYAREALIKE+J), because vicariance etc are disallowed, so the only way to have sisters with ranges (A,B) requires both a "d" and "e" event.  However, the BAYAREALIKE model has its own issues -- e.g. it is usually the worst-fitting base model.

4. Another option is to remove the null range from the state space, this is done in the "+*" models, e.g. DEC* (DECstar), discussed in Massana et al 2016 on bioRxiv:

Non-null Effects of the Null Range in Biogeographic Models - bioRxiv
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2015/09/16/026914

...Massana et al. show in simulations that this dramatically improves inference of "e". However, the "+x" solution has its own peculiarities, namely

4a. "e" often goes to infinity on empirical datasets (specifically, empirical datasets where most tips live in single areas, which is common...read Massana et al for why)
4b. Arguably, if AB->B is an allowed transition, then A->null should be allowed also
4c. It seems like changing the state space is "changing the data", and statistical model comparison requires fitting different models to identical data

As suggested in Massana et al., the real solution to the "e" problem is probably using a full SSE model, where instead of having transitions like A->null, instead you have a rate of lineage extinction for a lineage with range A (this suggestion goes back to Fitzjohn).  The complexity here is that for computation speed reasons, SSE models have only been run on fairly small state spaces, e.g. a few dozen states as of 2018.  In biogeography models we often have hundreds or thousands of states in the state space.

Anyhow: getting back to your question,

* The simple/crude way to answer it would just be to do Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping for your clade, count the number of different events through time, and then see if you observe an increase between when an area was thought increase in size.  Repeat over a collection of dated phylogenies to account for dating uncertainty.

* The best way would be to use a full SSE model and explicitly propose a model (e.g. in diversitree) where the speciation rate varies as a function of the area size through time, and see if you get statistical support for that over a null model where the speciation rate is independent.  However, I expect this would require a large tree (to have a chance of getting signal) and perhaps an SSE implementation that can scale up to a sufficient number of states, depending on the size of your state space.

Cheers,
Nick

> 1. Poor inference of "e" was noted in Ree & Smith 2008 for the DEC model
>
> 2. It seems to be similarly poor in most other models -- the basic problems are
>
> 2a. transitions like A->null and B->null are allowed in the model, but the "null range" is almost never observed in actual data.  As the null range is never observed, the inference "thinks" that the rate of going from A->null, B->null, etc., must be low, therefore "e" must be low (usually 0).  There are some exceptions, e.g. if you have many species occupying 2, 3, 4 etc. ranges, but this is fairly rare
>
> 2b. in a sense, the "e" process is competing with vicariance etc. as ways to "reduce range size", since the cladogenesis processes typically produce average ranges smaller than the parent range, it is hard to get signal for e
>
>
> 3. Inference of "e" probably works better in a model like BAYAREALIKE model (but not BAYAREALIKE+J), because vicariance etc are disallowed, so the only way to have sisters with ranges (A,B) requires both a "d" and "e" event.  However, the BAYAREALIKE model has its own issues -- e.g. it is usually the worst-fitting base model.
>
> 4. Another option is to remove the null range from the state space, this is done in the "+*" models, e.g. DEC* (DECstar), discussed in Massana et al 2016 on bioRxiv:
>
> Non-null Effects of the Null Range in Biogeographic Models - bioRxiv
> https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2015/09/16/026914
>
> ...Massana et al. show in simulations that this dramatically improves inference of "e". However, the "+x" solution has its own peculiarities, namely
>
> 4a. "e" often goes to infinity on empirical datasets (specifically, empirical datasets where most tips live in single areas, which is common...read Massana et al for why)
> 4b. Arguably, if AB->B is an allowed transition, then A->null should be allowed also
> 4c. It seems like changing the state space is "changing the data", and statistical model comparison requires fitting different models to identical data
>
>
> As suggested in Massana et al., the real solution to the "e" problem is probably using a full SSE model, where instead of having transitions like A->null, instead you have a rate of lineage extinction for a lineage with range A (this suggestion goes back to Fitzjohn).  The complexity here is that for computation speed reasons, SSE models have only been run on fairly small state spaces, e.g. a few dozen states as of 2018.  In biogeography models we often have hundreds or thousands of states in the state space.
>
> Anyhow: getting back to your question,
>
> * The simple/crude way to answer it would just be to do Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping for your clade, count the number of different events through time, and then see if you observe an increase between when an area was thought increase in size.  Repeat over a collection of dated phylogenies to account for dating uncertainty.
>
> * The best way would be to use a full SSE model and explicitly propose a model (e.g. in diversitree) where the speciation rate varies as a function of the area size through time, and see if you get statistical support for that over a null model where the speciation rate is independent.  However, I expect this would require a large tree (to have a chance of getting signal) and perhaps an SSE implementation that can scale up to a sufficient number of states, depending on the size of your state space.
>
> Cheers,
> Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I think I have figured out the optimx issue and why it was variable.

Basically:

1. The new 2018 version of "optimx" did not automatically install the package "minqa".  However, minqa was required for optimx ML searching with the "bobyqa" algorithm, which allows parameter searches with lower and upper bounds, and which is the algorithm that BioGeoBEARS-with-optimx was using.

2. For some reason, optimx does not report this problem, instead it just did one likelihood calculation, stopped the ML search after 1 step, and then returned NAs for the parameters

3. The NA parameters then caused a mysterious crash once the uppass calculations started.

Variability:

You wouldn't see this issue if you had the older optimx, or had minqa installed, or were using an optimizer other than optimx. (So, it would be most common on a "fresh install" of R and all packages)

The solutions:

1. I've put checks into BioGeoBEARS that check, if the 2018 version of optimx is being used, to check that minqa is installed. Also added a check for optimizers returning NA for parameters (in case there are future updates to the optimizer packages)

2. If you want to use optimx, you should do:

install.packages("minqa")

3. To get the code with the fix, do:

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS")

...or...

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS", INSTALL_opts="--byte-compile")

...if you want to try byte-compiling.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject_clean: (anonymized) fixnode analyses and lnL decreases
messages.body_plain:
Hi XXX!

A few thoughts...

XXX wrote:
> Hi Nick,
> thanks again for your suggestions. Everything worked perfect now, and I included you in the
> acknowledgments of the manuscript for your technical advices. One last question maybe regarding the
> fixnode analysis. The best-fit model has a worse LnL (-109.9) compared to the best-fit model of the
> unconstrained (-101.5) analysis (in both cases, DEC+J). I think this may be related to degrees of
> freedom, right?

I think of degrees of freedom as basically:

(degrees of freedom) = (number of data) - (number of free parameters estimated from the data)

...so it's not quite that.  Both the fixnode and non-fixnode analyses have the same number of free
parameters and the same tip data.

Really what is going on is this: a fixnode constraint will always lower the lnL, because, at that
node, you are taking:

the original likelihoods-of-the-data-above-the-node, e.g. A=0.1, B=0.15, AB=0.05

...and multiplying by the fixnode constraint:

(A=0.1, B=0.15, AB=0.05) x (0 1 0) --> (A=0, B=0.15, AB=0)

You've zeroed out some of the data likelihood, i.e. ruling out some of the scenarios that could have
explained the tip data.  Therefore the likelihood must go down.

Despite the decrease in likelihood, doing a fixnode analysis might be justifiable for various reasons:

* as adding more data -- fixing the states at a certain node is rather like adding another tip to a
tree, ie adding more data. Adding more data will always lower the likelihood as well (it's another
pattern that the model has to fit, and thus requires more events, each event has a probability cost)

* as reflecting a strong prior -- we aren't officially considering priors in a Maximum Likelihood
analysis, but it is reasonable to impose constraints on ancestor(s) range(s) if there is good evidence
justifying the prior

* as reflecting a hypothesis, e.g. you want to see how other ancestral ranges or parameter estimates
change, if you hypothesize that node-X-for-sure-had-range-B.

> In case that some reviewer is asking, why we prefer the fossil-constrained analysis which has a lower
> LnL is there anything to test between these two analyses such as with the +w models for the dispersal
> matrix (as in the Solanaceae paper by Dupin et al.) or is it just comparing apple with oranges and
> these two analyses should not be statistically compared at all?

They could be statistically compared (with AICc, not with LRT), but the comparison will show that the
more-constrained-fixnode-analysis has lower lnL!  But, it might be interesting to ask if the decrease
in model fit is substantial (roughly 2+ units of AICc) or not -- e.g., if the difference is low, then
this is evidence that the unconstrained analysis and the constrained analysis are roughly equally good
fits to the tip data.

> I think the latter is true and I would just compare differences in estimated ancestral areas, which
> are anyways only minor.

That is reasonable -- as with most variant analyses, it's all reasonable as long as you explain what
was done and why (or, that should be reasonable enough for reviewers...of course sometimes reviewers
disagree about what is reasonable)

Cheers!
Nick
